body:
The four traditions compared

Indian mural traditions are best distinguished through a combination of location, subject, architecture and visual characteristics.

The four sites studied here overlap in certain ways. Ajanta and Bagh share Buddhist associations, while Ajanta and Ellora are both in Maharashtra. Ellora and Lepakshi both contain Hindu religious imagery, but they belong to different architectural and artistic settings.

The following comparison brings together the most important identifying distinctions.

SiteLocationPrincipal associationImportant clue
AjantaMaharashtraBuddhist cave muralsShibi and Mahajanaka Jatakas; expressive, rounded figures
BaghMadhya PradeshBuddhist monastic paintingRang Mahal; courtly scenes, processions, musicians and dancers
ElloraMaharashtraBuddhist, Hindu and Jain rock-cut art34 caves; Kailasa; Jain cave paintings
LepakshiAndhra PradeshVijayanagara temple muralsVeerabhadra Temple; profile faces and prominent eyes

Geographical identification

Location is one of the most reliable clues because the four named sites belong to three different Indian states.

  • Maharashtra: Ajanta and Ellora.
  • Madhya Pradesh: Bagh.
  • Andhra Pradesh: Lepakshi.

Both Ajanta and Ellora belong to the western Deccan region of Maharashtra, but their principal artistic associations differ. Bagh represents a related classical mural tradition in central India, while Lepakshi illustrates the later Vijayanagara tradition of South India.

Distinguishing by historical period

The sites also represent different phases in the development of Indian art.

  • Ajanta: Early paintings date to approximately the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, while the most celebrated later paintings belong mainly to the 5th–6th centuries CE.
  • Bagh: Principal development is generally placed around the 4th–6th centuries CE.
  • Ellora: Major development of the principal monuments occurred broadly from the 6th to the 10th centuries CE.
  • Lepakshi: The major Vijayanagara-period temple murals belong to the 16th century CE.

These dates are useful approximations rather than exact dates for every individual painting. Different parts of a large historical site may have been created or decorated at different times.

Recognising paintings through subject and style

Buddhist Jataka narratives

A painting describing an earlier birth of the Bodhisattva is associated with the Buddhist narrative tradition.

If the subject specifically includes King Shibi protecting a dove or King Mahajanaka and Queen Sivali, Ajanta is the appropriate association among the four sites.

Expressive courtly and social scenes

The Bagh paintings are especially known for scenes involving musicians, dancers, processions and courtly life.

However, such themes are not exclusive to Bagh. Ajanta also contains courtly scenes, particularly within Jataka narratives. The location or cave name must therefore be considered before making a final identification.

Multiple religious traditions in one cave complex

A cave complex associated with Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism points strongly to Ellora.

The identification becomes decisive when the question includes Kailasa Cave 16, Jain Cave 32 or the classification of 34 numbered caves.

Vijayanagara temple painting

A painting from a Hindu temple in Andhra Pradesh, showing narratives from the Ramayana, Mahabharata or Shaivite tradition together with profile faces and prominent eyes, points towards Lepakshi.

The name Veerabhadra Temple or the historical association with the 16th-century Vijayanagara period makes this identification stronger.

Visual identification at a glance

Important distinctions to remember

  • Ajanta and Bagh: Both have Buddhist associations, but Ajanta is especially important for extensive Jataka narratives, while Bagh is distinguished by Rang Mahal and its lively social subjects.
  • Ajanta and Ellora: Both are in Maharashtra. Ajanta is principally associated with Buddhist murals; Ellora has monuments of three religious traditions.
  • Ellora and Lepakshi: Both contain Hindu religious art, but Ellora is a multi-religious rock-cut complex, whereas Lepakshi is a Vijayanagara temple site.
  • Shibi and Mahajanaka: Both are associated with Ajanta. Shibi highlights extraordinary self-sacrifice; Mahajanaka illustrates royal life and eventual renunciation.
  • Mural and sculpture: Both may occur in the same monument, but a carved stone relief is not itself a mural painting.

Four strong identification clues

  • Shibi or Mahajanaka: Ajanta.
  • Rang Mahal: Bagh.
  • Three religious cave groups: Ellora.
  • Vijayanagara profile figures: Lepakshi.

Prelims focus

  • Ajanta: Maharashtra; Buddhist Jatakas; Shibi and Mahajanaka.
  • Bagh: Madhya Pradesh; Rang Mahal, Cave 4; Buddhist murals with courtly subjects.
  • Ellora: Maharashtra; 34 principal caves; Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments.
  • Lepakshi: Andhra Pradesh; Veerabhadra Temple; Vijayanagara murals.
  • Shibi: Compassion and extraordinary self-sacrifice.
  • Mahajanaka: Kingship, Queen Sivali and eventual renunciation.
  • Trap: A single visual subject, such as a dancer or a royal court, is not always enough to identify a painting. Combine it with location, context and other distinctive features.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art Part-I, Class 11, chapters 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', pp. 37–43, and 'Later Mural Traditions', pp. 64–65; Archaeological Survey of India, 'Ajanta Caves' and 'Ellora Caves' (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Bagh Cave Paintings', Tentative List reference 7043, and 'Sri Veerabhadra Temple and Monolithic Bull (Nandi), Lepakshi', Tentative List reference 6607 (consulted 23 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Authentic murals from Ajanta, Bagh, Ellora and Lepakshi compare Buddhist narratives, expressive figures, Jain decoration and Vijayanagara profiles.
pictures.caption: Recognising four Indian mural traditions through their surviving art.

data.description: Four labelled photos of original surviving murals: Ajanta Cave 1, Mahajanaka Jataka; Bagh, associated with Cave 4 (Rang Mahal), expressive figures; Ellora Cave 32 (Indra Sabha), Jain decoration; Lepakshi Veerabhadra Temple, Vijayanagara profiles and prominent eyes. No reconstructions.

title: Identifying Ajanta, Bagh, Ellora and Lepakshi in Prelims
